VBO:0000663.summary: Lively and quick to notice change, Danish-Swedish Farmdogs have long been useful companions around the yard. They caught rats, watched the household, and stayed involved in daily farm life on both sides of the Øresund.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Danish-Swedish Farmdog
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: long-established Danish/Swedish farm watchdog, ratter and companion, recognized in 1987; temperament: alert, attentive and lively. The FCI standard gives Denmark and Sweden, 1987 recognition, farm watchdog/ratter/companion roles, compact rectangular form, and late maturity.

VBO:0200003.summary: Alert and persistent, the Affenpinscher began as a house dog in southern Germany and retains a watchful streak. It tends to meet unfamiliar activity with bold curiosity and can react quickly when something demands attention. Its ancestors appeared in Albrecht Dürer’s woodcuts centuries before the modern breed took shape.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Affenpinscher
sources.evidence: FCI temperament: fearless, alert, persistent, devoted, sometimes quick-tempered; historical summary: southern German house dog and Dürer woodcuts. The FCI standard gives southern German house-dog origins, rough coat, compact square build, facial hair, and the 1879 and Dürer references.

VBO:0200003.historicalRoots: Southern German house dog and companion.

VBO:0200010.summary: Composed and attentive, the Akita carries a Japanese history that began with the Matagi hunting dogs of the Akita region. Nineteenth-century crosses changed the breed’s size before breeders restored its spitz character. The present-day Akita tends to form a faithful bond and respond with a quiet, receptive manner around familiar people.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Akita
sources.evidence: FCI history: Akita Matagi origins and nineteenth-century crosses; temperament: composed, faithful, docile and receptive. The FCI Akita standard recounts Matagi roots, nineteenth-century crossing and restoration of spitz type, and describes body, ears, tail, and permitted colors.

VBO:0200010.historicalRoots: Japanese Matagi roots and later spitz restoration.

VBO:0200023.summary: Friendly in company but fearless on a difficult track, the Alpine Dachsbracke is a determined Austrian scent hunter. It follows wounded deer and pursues hare or fox through steep country, relying on a sensitive nose and weather endurance rather than outright speed. Its persistence is a working trait, not simply a high-energy manner.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Alpine Dachsbracke
sources.evidence: FCI utilization: weather-resistant mountain tracking of wounded deer and scent hunting of hare/fox; temperament: friendly expression and fearless personality. The FCI standard specifies Austrian origin, mountain tracking work, short-legged robust build, dense coat, and Rudolf’s 1881 and 1885 trips.

VBO:0200023.interestingFact: Crown Prince Rudolf took Alpine Dachsbracken on hunting trips to Turkey and Egypt in the 1880s.

VBO:0200046.summary: Lively and attentive, the American Eskimo Dog often takes an active interest in whatever its people are doing. It tends to be loyal and friendly with familiar people while taking time to warm to strangers; that alertness also made it a useful household watcher.

sources.title: Official breed standard: American Eskimo Dog
sources.evidence: UKC characteristics: intelligent, alert, energetic, loyal and friendly but sometimes conservative with strangers; standard also defines three sizes and German Spitz ancestry. The UKC standard describes German Spitz ancestry, American development, the name change, three size varieties, white or biscuit-cream coat, ears, and tail.

VBO:0200046.interestingFact: The name “American Eskimo Dog” replaced “American Spitz” during the First World War era.
VBO:0200046.historicalRoots: American development from German Spitz dogs.

VBO:0200055.summary: Often confident and good-natured with familiar people, the American Staffordshire Terrier also brings courage and alert curiosity to demanding activity. It tends to be intelligent and agile, with a strong interest in its surroundings.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: American Staffordshire Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI general appearance: muscular, agile, graceful, keenly alive to surroundings; temperament line says courage is proverbial. The FCI standard gives U.S. origin, muscular yet agile and graceful build, broad head, short coat, and preferred height ranges.

sources.title: American Kennel Club American Staffordshire Terrier breed profile
sources.evidence: AKC describes AmStaffs as smart, confident, good-natured companions and calls out their courage.

VBO:0200068.summary: Lively, vigilant, and quick to learn, the Appenzeller Sennenhund brings an all-rounder’s energy to farm life. Swiss farmers used it to drive cattle, watch the homestead, and sound an alarm when something changed. It tends to be deeply attached to familiar people while showing some reserve toward strangers.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Appenzeller Sennenhund
sources.evidence: FCI utilization: cattle driving, watch, guard, farm work; temperament: lively, self-assured, capable of learning, slightly suspicious of strangers. The FCI standard gives Swiss origin, cattle-driving and watch roles, tricolor nearly square build, curled tail, and the 1853 historical mention.

VBO:0200068.interestingFact: An Appenzell cattle dog was described in an 1853 book about Alpine animal life.

VBO:0200083.summary: Loyal to familiar people and attentive to unfamiliar movement, the Aidi developed as a guardian in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains. It watched camps, belongings, and flocks against predators, a protective role distinct from moving sheep. That work called for both close attachment to a household and independent judgment at the edge of its territory.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Aidi (Atlas Mountain Dog)
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: guards tents, possessions and flocks, explicitly not a European-style herder; temperament: faithful to family and discriminating protector. The FCI standard identifies Morocco and Atlas pastoral communities; describes protection of tents and flocks, thick coat, and says the breed did not herd flocks in the European sense.

VBO:0200095.summary: Keenly attentive and ready to respond, the Australian Shepherd was developed for long days of herding on American ranches. Its strong stock instinct shows in the way it notices small shifts in movement and works closely with a handler. Despite the name, the modern breed took shape in the United States, linked to Basque sheepherders arriving via Australia.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Australian Shepherd
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: U.S. ranch shepherd and Basque association; temperament: intelligent with herding and guarding instincts, stamina for all-day work, sometimes reserved at first meeting. The FCI standard identifies U.S. development, western ranch use, Basque shepherd association, proportions, coat colors, and farm-herding role.

VBO:0200100.summary: Persistent and agreeable, the Austrian Black and Tan Hound works a scent trail with a voice that lets hunters follow its course. It pursues hare and also tracks wounded game through mountains and lower country. A sensitive nose and willingness to keep at a difficult trail give the breed its distinctive hunting partnership.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Austrian Black and Tan Hound
sources.evidence: FCI utilization: hare hunting with voice and wounded-game tracking in mountains or flat country; behavior: sensitive nose, willing tracking and agreeable temperament. The FCI standard gives Austrian origin, hare and wounded-game work, mountain and flat-ground use, medium size, supple body, and black-and-tan markings.

VBO:0200100.historicalRoots: Austrian scenthound for hare and wounded game.

VBO:0200118.summary: Cheerful and willing, the Barbado da Terceira tends to learn quickly and stay close to familiar people. On its home island in the Azores, it gathered cattle and watched the farm.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Barbado da Terceira
sources.evidence: Portuguese kennel club use: cattle driving, guard and companion; temperament: faithful, intelligent, easy to teach, cheerful, gentle and willing. The Portuguese Kennel Club identifies Terceira Island origin, cattle-driving and guard functions, and describes the bearded, abundant-coated working form.

VBO:0200118.historicalRoots: Terceira Island cattle and farm dog.

VBO:0200125.summary: Sociable and affectionate with familiar people, the Basset Fauve de Bretagne is also a notably persistent scent hunter. It pursues quarry from rabbit to wild boar through difficult ground, with more speed and stamina than its low stature suggests. Its working roots lead to the larger Griffon Fauve de Bretagne.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Basset Fauve de Bretagne
sources.evidence: FCI utilization: hunts rabbit, hare, fox, roe deer and boar; temperament: passionate, courageous, wily and obstinate hunter, sociable and affectionate companion. The FCI standard gives Breton ancestry, game pursued, fawn wiry coat, low sturdy build, and regional-to-national history.

VBO:0200125.interestingFact: The breed spread beyond Brittany in the late twentieth century after a long period of strong regional popularity.
VBO:0200125.historicalRoots: Brittany scenthound descended from the Griffon Fauve.

VBO:0200134.summary: Lively and confident, Bearded Collies bring steady initiative to the job of moving sheep. They spent centuries in Scotland and northern England doing work that rewarded alertness without losing the balance of a practical herding dog. Sixteenth-century Scottish records already mention dogs resembling this worker.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bearded Collie
sources.evidence: FCI history: sheep herding in Scotland/northern England with sixteenth-century references; temperament: alert, lively, self-confident, active and steady. The FCI standard describes Scottish and northern English sheep-herding roots, sixteenth-century records, lean active build, and long harsh coat with facial furnishings.

VBO:0200154.summary: Patient and attentive around the flock, Bergamasco Shepherd Dogs were shaped by seasonal sheep movements through northern Italian valleys. Driving and guarding herds called for concentration and decisions made close to the animals. They tend to be strongly connected to their own people, giving their independent work a human anchor.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bergamasco Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: Alpine transhumance, driving and guarding herds; temperament: vigilance, concentration, determination, patience and close human relationship. The FCI standard identifies Bergamo-area transhumance, herd-driving and guarding, square build, and three hair types forming flocks.

VBO:0200154.historicalRoots: Italian Alpine herd work and seasonal sheep movement.

VBO:0200163.summary: Sociable and ready to share household routines, the Bichon Frise has spent centuries in close human company. It tends to meet people and other dogs cheerfully, while frequent barking is not typical of the breed. Its companion history runs from Renaissance France into later European homes.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bichon Frise
sources.evidence: FCI history: Italy to Renaissance France and court portraits; temperament: sociable with people/dogs, adaptable, attached, not often barking. The FCI standard gives Franco-Belgian patronage, Italian-to-French Renaissance history, court portraiture, the barbichon etymology, and white curled coat.

VBO:0200163.interestingFact: The name “bichon” developed from “barbichon,” a comparison to a tiny Barbet.
VBO:0200163.historicalRoots: European companion dog with Renaissance court history.

VBO:0200175.summary: Gentle and sociable in company, the Bloodhound can become intensely persistent when a scent trail takes hold. Its extraordinary nose and staying power served large-game hunts and later searches for missing people. Saint-Hubert monks in the Belgian Ardennes helped shape this remarkable working hound.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bloodhound
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: wounded-game and missing-person tracking over long distances, Saint-Hubert abbey; temperament: gentle, placid, sociable and somewhat stubborn. The FCI standard identifies Belgian Saint-Hubert history, human-scent tracking use, large substantial build, loose skin, and long low-set ears.

VBO:0200193.summary: Keenly attentive and quick to learn, the Border Collie was selected to read moving sheep and respond precisely to a handler. It tends to persist when a task holds its interest, bringing both stamina and responsiveness to long days with stock.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Border Collie
sources.evidence: FCI use: sheepdog; temperament: tenacious, hard-working, tractable, keen, alert, responsive and intelligent. The FCI standard identifies British sheepdog use, balanced outline, body proportions, smooth and rough coats, broad color range, and white-color limit.

VBO:0200193.historicalRoots: British sheepdog selected for stock work.

VBO:0200204.summary: Lively and friendly, the Boston Terrier tends to notice and join household activity with bright curiosity. It developed in the United States as a close companion, and intelligence and a sociable disposition remain central to its identity.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Boston Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI utilization: companion; temperament: friendly, lively, intelligent and excellent disposition. The FCI standard states U.S. origin, companion use, head and body form, short tail, permitted colors, white pattern, movement, and the meaning of seal.

VBO:0200214.summary: Eager and attentive in the field, the Boykin Spaniel works closely with a handler across land and water. South Carolina hunters needed a dog that could ride in a narrow boat yet find, flush, and retrieve birds in swamp country. That unusually specific partnership earned it the nickname “little brown dog that doesn’t rock the boat.”

sources.title: AKC Official Standard for the Boykin Spaniel
sources.evidence: The AKC standard identifies South Carolina as the breed origin and describes a compact, agile flushing dog developed for use in small boats on local waterways.

sources.title: AKC Boykin Spaniel history
sources.evidence: AKC history documents South Carolina swamp hunting, bird retrieval across land and water, the small-boat role, and the “little brown dog that doesn’t rock the boat” nickname.

VBO:0200214.interestingFact: The Boykin Spaniel is the state dog of South Carolina.
VBO:0200214.historicalRoots: South Carolina waterfowl and upland hunting spaniel.

VBO:0200234.summary: Courageous and composed, Briards brought steady nerves as well as initiative to generations of French flock work. They drove and guarded sheep in the lowlands, then supported the French army during both world wars. Their ability to stay engaged with demanding human work is as important to the breed’s history as its pastoral roots.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Briard
sources.evidence: FCI utilization/history: French sheep driving and guarding, French army use in both world wars; temperament: steady, fearless, balanced. The FCI standard gives French lowland herding and guard work, 1809 name reference, wartime roles, supple build, long coat, and double rear dewclaws.

VBO:0200234.interestingFact: French forces also used Briards during both world wars for duties that included carrying supplies and finding wounded soldiers.

VBO:0200258.summary: Bold and affectionate, the Bulldog carries a difficult British history behind its present companion role. Bull-baiting shaped the early breed before the practice ended; later breeders kept the determination while emphasizing a calmer household manner. That change of purpose is one of the sharpest turns in any breed’s story.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Bulldog
sources.evidence: FCI history: bull-baiting until after 1835 and later companion development; temperament: determined, alert, bold, loyal, affectionate. The FCI standard describes early bull-baiting, post-1835 change, broad compact form, movement and breathing safeguards, and 1630s naming.

VBO:0200258.interestingFact: The name “Bulldog” was in use by the 1630s.
VBO:0200258.historicalRoots: British bull-baiting history followed by companion breeding.

VBO:0200270.summary: Lively and versatile, the Calupoh tends to bond closely with its family while taking time to warm to strangers. It is described as agile and stable in manner, a blend that suits an attentive companion. Its modern Mexican identity draws on a much older cultural fascination with wolf-dog crosses in pre-Hispanic Mexico.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Calupoh
sources.evidence: Mexican kennel federation standard: agile, dynamic, stable, loyal to family, possibly aloof with strangers; historical summary: pre-Hispanic wolf-dog symbolism and archaeological finds. The Mexican national standard describes the modern companion wolfdog, tall dark-coated form, and archaeological evidence of symbolic wolf-dog crosses.

VBO:0200270.historicalRoots: Modern Mexican wolfdog breed with pre-Hispanic cultural references.

VBO:0200274.summary: Watchful and quick to react, the Canaan Dog tends to bond closely with its own people while remaining wary of strangers. Its Middle Eastern history includes security and warning work, where noticing unfamiliar people or animals mattered. Alertness and a willingness to learn give that guarded manner a practical focus.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Canaan Dog
sources.evidence: FCI use: watch and security; temperament: alert, quick to react, wary of strangers, defensive but not naturally aggressive, devoted and trainable. The FCI standard gives Israel as origin, watch and security use, square medium body, erect ears, curled tail, primitive type, and color range.

VBO:0200274.historicalRoots: Middle Eastern watch and security dog.

VBO:0200304.summary: Self-assured and watchful, Caucasian Shepherd Dogs tend to make independent judgments while staying closely attached to their own people. Their guarding history across the Caucasus and southern Russian steppe called for resolve through harsh weather and real threats. Modern selection began in the Soviet Union in the 1920s, but the pastoral role is much older.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Caucasian Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Caucasian and southern Russian guard work; temperament: steady, self-confident, fearless, independent and devoted to owner; Soviet selection history. The FCI standard gives Caucasian and southern Russian distribution, guard roles, massive build, double coat, climatic hardiness, and Soviet selection history.

VBO:0200323.summary: Cheerful and calm with familiar people, the Cesky Terrier can be reserved at first with strangers. František Horák developed the breed in the Czech Republic from Scottish and Sealyham terriers for fox and badger hunting. Its more manageable working manner was part of the purpose behind that deliberate postwar cross.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Cesky Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: fox and badger hunting, Horák’s 1949 Scottish–Sealyham program; temperament: balanced, cheerful, calm, kind, reserved with strangers. The FCI standard names Horák, 1949, the Scottish–Sealyham cross, fox and badger purpose, drop ears, rectangular body, and soft clipped coat.

VBO:0200351.summary: Calm, independent, and closely loyal to its own family, the Chinese Shar-Pei carries a quiet form of watchfulness. Earlier dogs in southern China hunted and guarded property, work that rewarded attention and resolve.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Chinese Shar-Pei
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: southern Chinese hunting and watch dog; temperament: calm, independent, loyal and affectionate to family. The FCI standard identifies South China Sea origins, hunting and watch use, square body, wrinkles, small ears, muzzle, and harsh short coat.

sources.title: American Kennel Club Chinese Shar-Pei breed profile
sources.evidence: AKC gives the literal sand-skin translation of Shar-Pei and describes its harsh, sandpapery coat.

VBO:0200351.historicalRoots: Southern Chinese hunting and watch dog.

VBO:0200361.summary: Quiet and self-possessed, Chow Chows tend to be loyal to familiar people yet reserved when meeting strangers. They guarded homes and accompanied hunts in China long before the breed reached Britain. That measured manner helps explain why their watchfulness can be easy to underestimate.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Chow Chow
sources.evidence: FCI history: Chinese guarding and hunting before spread to Britain; temperament: quiet, good guard, independent, loyal and aloof. The FCI standard gives Chinese guard and hunting history, arrival in other countries around 1800, leonine shape, tail, tongue, and movement safeguards.

VBO:0200366.summary: Steady and kindly, the Clumber Spaniel often works with more deliberation than other spaniels. It flushes game quietly through cover, trusting an excellent nose rather than speed, and can be somewhat reserved when first meeting people. The breed’s history is tied to Clumber Park in Nottinghamshire; patience is part of both its work and its manner.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Clumber Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: flushing dog at Clumber Park, steady pace; temperament: silent worker with excellent nose, stoical, kind, steady and relatively aloof. The FCI standard cites Clumber Park, a possible French antecedent, heavy body, slower working pace, white coat, flushing role, and quiet scent work.

VBO:0200366.historicalRoots: British flushing spaniel associated with Clumber Park.

VBO:0200402.summary: Quick to react and deeply loyal to familiar people, the Czechoslovakian Wolfdog is also noted for stamina and caution around strangers. It began in a 1955 Czechoslovakian working experiment crossing German Shepherd Dogs with Carpathian wolves.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Czechoslovakian Wolfdog
sources.evidence: FCI history: 1955 Shepherd–Carpathian wolf crossings; temperament: active, enduring, quick-reacting, fearless, suspicious and loyal. The FCI standard details the 1955 crosses in Czechoslovakia, both mating directions, working purpose, rectangular build, gray coat, and light mask.

VBO:0200402.interestingFact: Both male-dog-to-female-wolf and male-wolf-to-female-dog matings were used in the original experiment.
VBO:0200402.historicalRoots: Czechoslovakian working breed founded in 1955 wolf-dog crosses.

VBO:0200447.summary: Calm and loyal with familiar people, the Dogo Guatemalteco may scrutinize strangers before relaxing when they are welcomed. It developed in Guatemala for protection, service, and companionship from a mix that included large Bull Terriers, Boxers, and Dalmatians. Family loyalty and alert guarding remain central to its character.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Dogo Guatemalteco
sources.evidence: Guatemalan standard: protection/service use, formation breeds; temperament: calm, affectionate and loyal to family, cautious with strangers, alert in guard work. The Guatemalan canine association standard gives origin, early formation breeds, former name, use, white coat, and muscular head and body.

VBO:0200447.interestingFact: For much of the twentieth century the breed was known as the Guatemalan Bull Terrier.
VBO:0200447.historicalRoots: Guatemalan protection and service dog developed in the early twentieth century.

VBO:0200454.summary: Keen but even-tempered, the Drever brings steady persistence to a scent trail rather than a burst of speed. It follows deer at a pace that lets hunters keep up on foot and continues working over long tracks and difficult ground. Sweden developed the breed from Westphalian Dachsbrackes for this practical hunting style.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Drever
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Swedish deer tracker from Westphalian Dachsbracke imports; temperament: keen and even; low stature supports foot-hunting pace. The FCI standard traces Westphalian imports to 1910, deer-tracking use, short strong body, and adoption of the name Drever in 1947.

VBO:0200454.historicalRoots: Swedish deer-tracking hound from Westphalian Dachsbracke stock.

VBO:0200486.summary: Gentle and affectionate with familiar people, English Cocker Spaniels can become bustling, enthusiastic workers on a scent. They took their name from woodcock, the birds they once flushed from thick cover. Working and show lines differ today, but the impulse to investigate a trail still links them.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: English Cocker Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: woodcock flushing and working/show lines; temperament: merry, bustling on scent, fearless of heavy cover, gentle and affectionate. The FCI standard explains woodcock naming, separation from Field and Springer spaniels, flushing role, compact build, and working/show distinction.

VBO:0200497.summary: Eager and cooperative, English Springer Spaniels tend to work closely with a handler when finding and flushing game. Before guns changed the hunt, their ancestors sprang birds for nets, falcons, or greyhounds; the breed later became a flushing and retrieving gun dog. Its active nature is rooted in that long partnership in the field.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: English Springer Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: springing game for net, falcon or greyhound, later flushing and retrieving for gun; temperament: friendly, happy and biddable. The FCI standard describes pre-gun springing work, present flushing and retrieving, compact athletic build, and comparative leg length.

VBO:0200509.summary: Close to their own shepherd and cautious with strangers, Estrela Mountain Dogs bring an attentive judgment to flock protection. They traveled with Portuguese flocks between valley and high pasture, guarding against predators and thieves.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Estrela Mountain Dog
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: livestock guarding, seasonal mountain pasture, two coat varieties; temperament: faithful to shepherd, brave protector, wary of strangers and docile with owner. The FCI standard gives the Estrela region, livestock guarding, seasonal ascent, two coat varieties, and large balanced build.

VBO:0200509.interestingFact: Traditional summer pasture in the Estrela Mountains can reach roughly 2,000 meters.

VBO:0200520.summary: Calm and self-assured with familiar people, the Fila Brasileiro is also markedly vigilant in unfamiliar situations. Its Brazilian history combines watching, protection, and the courage to face large game. Steady nerves and alert judgment mattered as much as force in those demanding working roles.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Fila Brasileiro
sources.evidence: FCI use: watch dog and big-game hunting; temperament: courageous, determined, calm, self-assured, loyal to family, vigilant guardian. The FCI standard gives Brazilian origin, watch-dog use, rectangular molosser build, loose skin, agility, and characteristic gait.

VBO:0200529.summary: Keenly alert and quick to react, the Formosan Mountain Dog retains the attention valued in Taiwan’s central mountain hunting dogs. Its roots trace to dogs that accompanied hunters through forest terrain, where noticing movement and keeping up with people mattered. The breed’s native identity was documented again in a 1980 university survey.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Formosan Mountain Dog
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: central Taiwan hunting companions and 1980 university survey; temperament: faithful, keen-sensed, alert, bold and fearless. The FCI Taiwan Dog standard identifies mountain hunting roots, wedge head, erect ears, sickle tail, medium build, and the 1980 university survey.

VBO:0200557.summary: Serious or reserved away from the chase, the Galgo Español becomes lively and energetic in hunting work. This Spanish sighthound was shaped by open-field hare pursuit, where keen sight and sustained effort mattered. The contrast between quiet company and determined coursing is a memorable part of its character.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Galgo Español
sources.evidence: FCI use: open-field hare pursuit by sight; temperament: serious and sometimes reserved, energetic and lively when hunting. The FCI standard gives Spain, open-field hare coursing, long narrow form, chest and tail, and two coat textures.

VBO:0200577.summary: Steadily attentive and willing to work beside a handler, the German Shepherd Dog grew from versatile German herding stock. Its role expanded into protection and other service work, asking for focus in changing situations. That ability to shift tasks while remaining responsive to human direction is central to its working identity.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: German Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI use: versatile working, herding and service dog; character: self-assured, attentive, willing to please, resilient; historical German breed organization. The FCI standard describes German breed organization, 1899 club founding, herding and service roles, proportions, trot, ears, and coat varieties.

VBO:0200604.summary: Energetic yet composed, the Giant Schnauzer tends to bring loyalty and endurance to demanding work. It first drove cattle in southern Germany and later took on broader utility roles. Its capacity to stay focused through a long task grew alongside a close working partnership with people.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Giant Schnauzer
sources.evidence: FCI history: southern German cattle driver, stud book 1913, working recognition 1925; temperament: even, loyal, trainable, strong and enduring. The FCI standard gives southern German cattle work, square powerful build, wiry coat and furnishings, 1913 registration, and 1925 working recognition.

VBO:0200604.historicalRoots: Southern German cattle driving and later utility work.

VBO:0200615.summary: Courageous and independent on a scent trail, the Grand Basset Griffon Vendéen makes its progress known with a ringing voice. It was selected to pursue hare through the brambles and scrub of western France, working with speed as well as persistence in cover. Paul Dezamy helped establish the working type behind this distinctive hound.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Grand Basset Griffon Vendeen
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: hare hunter in scrub/bramble, selected by Paul Dezamy; temperament: fast, vocal, passionate, courageous and a little stubborn. The FCI standard describes origin from larger griffons, Paul Dezamy’s hare-hunting selection, straight legs, low long body, rough coat, and voiced work.

VBO:0200615.historicalRoots: Vendéen hare hound refined from larger griffons.

VBO:0200636.summary: Bold and energetic in Arctic work, Greenland Dogs can also be friendly toward people, including strangers. Inuit communities selected them for the mental toughness and endurance needed to pull sledges, while a strong hunting instinct served seal and polar-bear hunts. Their story joins transport, hunting, and close human cooperation.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Greenland Dog
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Inuit sledge dog and seal/polar-bear hunting; temperament: energetic, mentally strong, bold, tireless and friendly to people including strangers. The FCI standard gives Inuit sledge-dog history, polar work, dense coat, erect ears, tail, and size flexibility.

VBO:0200662.summary: Playful and affectionate, the Havanese tends to take an active interest in household life. Its quickness to learn once suited a little alarm dog, while its close companion role took shape in Cuban homes. Earlier Bichon-type ancestors crossed from the western Mediterranean before that cheerful, people-focused island tradition developed.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Havanese
sources.evidence: FCI history: western Mediterranean Bichon-type dogs developed in Cuba; temperament: affectionate, happy, playful, quick to train as alarm dog. The FCI standard identifies western Mediterranean ancestry, development in Cuba, companion use, low sturdy frame, soft wavy coat, and elastic movement.

VBO:0200662.historicalRoots: Mediterranean Bichon ancestry developed in Cuba.

VBO:0200674.summary: Confident and devoted to familiar people, the Hovawart retains the protective attention of an old German estate watcher. Rebuilt as a breed from farm dogs in the twentieth century, it also developed a useful nose for tracking and rescue work. The name itself points to the farmyard or property it once guarded.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Hovawart
sources.evidence: FCI name/history: German estate watcher rebuilt from farm dogs after 1922; temperament/use: good nose, tracking/rescue, protective, devoted and self-confident. The FCI standard explains the name, 1922 reconstruction and crosses, estate-guardian roots, long coat, and powerful proportions.

VBO:0200674.interestingFact: The revival program used, among others, German Shepherd Dogs, Newfoundlands, and Leonbergers.
VBO:0200674.historicalRoots: German farm and estate guardian rebuilt in the twentieth century.

VBO:0200688.summary: Keenly alert to sound, scent, and movement, Ibizan Hounds hunt rabbits across the Balearic Islands with more than sight alone. When one dog finds quarry, others can join the search, turning pursuit into coordinated work over rocky ground and dense cover. That sensory range and cooperation make their island hunting tradition distinctive.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Ibizan Hound
sources.evidence: FCI utilization: Balearic rabbit hunting by scent and hearing, individual and coordinated pack work, agility through dense cover. The FCI standard identifies Balearic origins, rabbit hunting by scent and hearing, pack behavior, tall narrow form, and pricked ears.

VBO:0200696.summary: Indian Spitz is a spitz-family companion familiar in Indian homes, with its own place in the country’s dog-show world. The Andhra Pradesh Kennel Club lists it among native breeds, while the Indian National Kennel Club has argued for recognizing Spitz separately from Pomeranian and Samoyed registrations. Its local identity has endured despite inconsistent naming between clubs.

sources.title: Indian Veterinary Research Institute study of Indian Spitz dogs
sources.evidence: The 2019 Indian Veterinary Research Institute original study identifies Indian Spitz as a spitz-family companion in India and reports a cohort of 24 owner-kept dogs.

sources.title: Andhra Pradesh Kennel Club 2017 show schedule
sources.evidence: The official schedule lists Indian Spitz by name within the Native Breeds show group.

sources.title: Indian National Kennel Club overview
sources.evidence: INKC says it has long recognized Spitz separately and describes registrations by other clubs under Pomeranian, Samoyed and later names.

VBO:0200706.summary: Gentle and friendly with people and other dogs, the Irish Wolfhound carries a much fiercer hunting past. It once pursued wolves, boar, and deer in Ireland, demanding both courage and reach in the chase. An old saying captures the contrast between quiet companionship and historic pursuit: a lamb at home and a lion in the chase.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Irish Wolfhound
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: wolves, boar and deer hunting in Ireland; temperament: gentle, kind, loyal and friendly with people and other dogs; includes lamb/lion saying. The FCI standard gives Irish wolf, deer, and boar hunting, tall rough-coated sighthound form, movement, and the 391 written reference.

VBO:0200706.interestingFact: One of the earliest written accounts of Irish wolfhounds dates to 391 CE.

VBO:0200713.summary: Lively and affectionate in close company, Italian Greyhounds also carry the swift reactions of a sighthound. Their history reaches into Renaissance Italian courts, where their intimate companion role existed alongside athletic instinct. That combination of movement and closeness to people has defined the breed for centuries.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Italian Greyhound
sources.evidence: FCI history: small Mediterranean sighthounds developed in Italian Renaissance courts; use: racing dog; temperament: lively, affectionate and docile. The FCI standard describes Mediterranean ancestry, arrival in Italy, Renaissance court prominence, square miniature-sighthound proportions, and fine coat.

VBO:0200713.interestingFact: Renaissance paintings frequently placed these small sighthounds beside nobles.
VBO:0200713.historicalRoots: Small Mediterranean sighthound developed in Italy.

VBO:0200732.summary: Bold and persistent on quarry, the Jagdterrier can also be sociable and trainable with familiar people. German hunters created the breed after the First World War for demanding work above and below ground. Its willingness to press through difficult cover shows the intensity for which it was selected.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Jagdterrier
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: post-WWI German hunting program, underground hunting and flushing; temperament: courageous, hard, enduring, work-loving, sociable and trainable. The FCI standard recounts the postwar German breeding program, black-and-tan selection, underground and flushing work, and compact coat varieties.

VBO:0200740.summary: Cheerful and keen-sensed, the Japanese Spitz tends to notice activity around the home quickly. It became a lively companion after spitz dogs were brought to Japan in the early twentieth century. Its alert interest in people and surroundings gives the breed an engaging everyday role beyond simply keeping company.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Japanese Spitz
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: imported white spitz dogs developed in Japan as companion; temperament: intelligent, cheerful and keen-sensed. The FCI standard gives Japanese development, early import history and 1921 exhibition, companion role, white coat, ears, tail, and proportions.

VBO:0200740.interestingFact: A white German Spitz imported via Siberia and northeast China was exhibited in Tokyo in 1921.
VBO:0200740.historicalRoots: Japanese white-spitz companion developed in the twentieth century.

VBO:0200749.summary: Steady and independently minded, the Kangal Dog tends to be affectionate with familiar people but wary of strangers while guarding. It watches sheep through heat, cold, and long quiet stretches in Turkey. The work calls for judgment about when an approaching animal or person actually needs a response.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Kangal Dog
sources.evidence: FCI use: Turkish sheep guardian working in heat/cold; temperament: steady, bold, independent, intelligent, loyal to owners and wary of strangers on duty. The FCI standard gives Turkish sheep-guarding use, cultural context, dark mask, thick coat, powerful rectangular form, and caution about ancient origins.

VBO:0200758.summary: Courageous and deeply attached to its own people, the Karst Shepherd Dog also retains an independent streak. It guarded flocks for centuries in Slovenia’s Karst region, staying alert to unfamiliar visitors while making its own decisions near the animals. A written mention of the type dates to 1689.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Karst Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Karst flock guarding, 1689 written reference; temperament: courageous, devoted, wary of strangers, obedient with strong individuality. The FCI standard gives Karst origin, shepherd and guard use, iron-gray long coat, hanging ears and tail, and Valvasor’s 1689 reference.

VBO:0200758.historicalRoots: Slovenian Karst flock and property guardian.

VBO:0200772.summary: Watchful and quick to learn, the Kintamani-Bali Dog tends to be gentle and loyal with familiar people. It comes from the highlands around Sukawana, where it has been kept as a close household companion. That mountain-village history is clear even though the breed’s earliest ancestry remains uncertain.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Kintamani-Bali Dog
sources.evidence: FCI history: native to Sukawana/Kintamani, early ancestry uncertain; use: companion; temperament: watchful, intelligent, alert, gentle, loyal and easy to train. The FCI standard identifies Sukawana/Kintamani origin, uncertain early history, household companion use, wedge head, ears, tail, and double coat.

VBO:0200779.summary: Decisive and distrustful of intruders, the Komondor tends to keep a particularly active watch after dark. Hungarian livestock guardians had to judge threats to a flock or property and act without constant direction. That independent night-guarding rhythm shaped the breed’s enduring character.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Komondor
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Magyar pastoral roots and herd/property defense; temperament: courageous, territorial, suspicious and active on night patrol. The FCI standard describes Magyar pastoral roots, Hungarian herding tradition, large powerful build, and dense matted corded coat.

VBO:0200779.interestingFact: The Komondor’s ancestors are associated with Magyar pastoral movements into the Carpathian Basin.

VBO:0200808.summary: Cheerful and affectionate with familiar people, the Lancashire Heeler also keeps a quick eye out for small quarry. It worked cattle in northwest England and turned the same brisk attention to rats and rabbits around the farm. Its exact ancestry remains uncertain, but that dual cattle-and-vermin role is well documented.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Lancashire Heeler
sources.evidence: FCI use/history: Ormskirk cattle work, rabbiting and ratting, uncertain ancestry; temperament: courageous, happy and affectionate to owner. The FCI standard gives Lancashire/Ormskirk roots, cattle and vermin work, short sturdy build, coat colors, and uncertain Welsh-dog/terrier ancestry.

VBO:0200808.interestingFact: Its proposed ancestry includes Welsh cattle dogs and Manchester Terriers, though the exact history remains unproven.
VBO:0200808.historicalRoots: Lancashire cattle and farm vermin work.

VBO:0200819.summary: Composed and playful around familiar people, the Leonberger became a steady companion and watch dog. Heinrich Essig developed it near Stuttgart in the nineteenth century, drawing on several giant working breeds. Its calm manner amid busy household life has remained central to the breed’s identity.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Leonberger
sources.evidence: FCI history: Essig’s nineteenth-century Leonberg breeding with Newfoundland, Saint Bernard-type and Pyrenean Mountain Dog; use/temperament: watch and companion, composed, playful, friendly. The FCI standard gives Essig’s nineteenth-century crosses, Leonberg origin, lion imagery, watch/companion role, mane, and balanced strong build.

VBO:0200819.historicalRoots: Nineteenth-century German giant companion and watchdog.

VBO:0200856.summary: Lively and affectionate near its people, the Maltese has long filled a close companion role around the Mediterranean. Maritime settlements figure in its history, though the exact route of its origins remains debated. Even its name carries a mystery, perhaps echoing an old word for harbor rather than referring only to Malta.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Maltese
sources.evidence: FCI history: Mediterranean maritime dogs and uncertain Malta-name origin; temperament: lively, affectionate, calm and intelligent. The FCI standard describes maritime Mediterranean antecedents, uncertain name origin, tiny long-bodied form, white long coat, and companion role.

VBO:0200867.summary: Calm and affectionate with familiar people, the Mastiff also retains the watchful courage of Britain’s long guard-dog tradition. Accounts of mastiff-type dogs reach back before Agincourt, but the breed’s present-day manner is often quiet and self-possessed. Its ability to notice a threat without constant agitation is a less visible part of its guardian character.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Mastiff
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: British mastiff-type dogs before Agincourt, watch/security role; temperament: calm, affectionate to owners, courageous guardian, generally indifferent to strangers. The FCI standard gives British history, watch use, giant square-headed structure, short coat and dark mask, and soundness requirement.

VBO:0200906.summary: Balanced and closely attached to its handler, the Montenegrin Mountain Hound brings steady persistence to a scent trail. It belongs to the Balkan tradition of hunting through rugged country, following quarry with a dependable working style.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Montenegrin Mountain Hound
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Balkan hound roots and hunting work; temperament: well balanced, attached to master, docile and trustworthy; old black-hound name. The FCI standard identifies Montenegro/Balkan hound roots, black-and-tan coloring, medium solid build, hunting role, old name, and 1924 standard.

VBO:0200930.summary: Steady and loyal, the Neapolitan Mastiff remains alert to activity around the home despite its often quiet manner. Its southern Italian history centers on property guarding around Naples and Mount Vesuvius. Ancient Roman mastiff associations add depth, but its long local guardian role is the clearest thread in the breed’s story.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Neapolitan Mastiff
sources.evidence: FCI history: Roman mastiff tradition and survival near Vesuvius; use: property guard; temperament: steady, loyal, vigilant and not aggressive. The FCI standard gives southern Italian/Vesuvius history, Roman-mastiff tradition, guard use, massive long body, and loose skin.

VBO:0200945.summary: Boldly curious yet companionable, the Norfolk Terrier brings a small hunter’s resolve to new activity. East Anglian farm dogs needed courage for vermin work in tight places; an old saying called the breed “a demon for its size.” Its shared farm history with the Norwich Terrier still explains its busy, persistent character.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Norfolk Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI history: East Anglian farm terrier shared with Norwich; temperament: alert, fearless, hardy, lovable and not quarrelsome; folded ears. The FCI standard recounts shared East Anglian farm-dog roots with Norwich, low compact build, harsh coat, and dropped ears.

VBO:0200945.historicalRoots: East Anglian farm and vermin terrier.

VBO:0200962.summary: Busy and fearless, Norwich Terriers also tend to be companionable with familiar people. They emerged from East Anglian farm dogs that hunted vermin wherever a small, tenacious worker could fit. That tireless interest in their surroundings outlasted the old farm setting and remains central to the breed’s character.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Norwich Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI history: East Anglian farm terrier shared with Norfolk; temperament: tremendously active, hardy, cheerful and fearless; erect ears. The FCI standard gives East Anglian shared history, small compact form, erect ears, harsh coat, and terrier background.

VBO:0200962.historicalRoots: East Anglian farm and vermin terrier.

VBO:0200969.summary: Steady, biddable, and bold, the Old English Sheepdog was a country worker before it became a familiar companion. Cooperation with people served sheep work through changing weather and long days.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Old English Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: British sheepdog, Bob-Tail name and weather-resistant working coat; temperament: biddable, even, bold, faithful and trustworthy. The FCI standard gives British sheepdog identity, Bob-Tail nickname, European ancestry hypothesis, profuse weatherproof coat, square body, and rolling gait.

VBO:0200969.historicalRoots: British country sheepdog with mixed historical roots.

VBO:0200994.summary: Fearless and loyal to familiar people, the Pekingese has a distinctly self-possessed manner. It was bred for companionship in China and tends to meet strangers with dignified reserve. That combination of closeness and independence gives the small dog a character that can feel larger than its size.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Pekingese
sources.evidence: FCI use/origin: Chinese companion; temperament: fearless, loyal, aloof, not timid or aggressive. The FCI standard gives Chinese origin, companion role, leonine appearance, broad head, low body, and safeguards for breathing, movement, and coat amount.

VBO:0201029.summary: Keenly aware of game and gentle in ordinary company, the Pointer combines field intensity with an even manner. It finds quarry and holds a still, directed point that tells a hunter exactly where to look. Endurance over long stretches of British hunting ground made that precise signal useful far beyond a brief burst of speed.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Pointer
sources.evidence: FCI use: pointing dog; temperament: alert with strength/endurance/speed, kind and even; field work requires locating and indicating game. The FCI standard identifies British pointing work, symmetrical curved outline, strong supple build, short coat, and endurance/speed.

VBO:0201043.summary: Attentive and lively, the Pomeranian tends to learn quickly and raise an alarm when household activity changes. It is the toy-sized German Spitz, sharing a family history with larger spitz dogs while carrying its own close companion role. Its alert interest in people and surroundings remains its defining everyday trait.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Pomeranian
sources.evidence: FCI Toy Spitz/Pomeranian section: attentive, lively, attached, teachable, cheerful, companion and household watch role; German Spitz family context. The FCI German Spitz standard names Toy Spitz/Pomeranian, German origin, watch and companion use, ruff, erect ears, tail, and standing double coat.

VBO:0201067.summary: Watchful and resourceful, the Portuguese Podengo is a family of hunting dogs rather than one fixed working style. Large Podengos pursued bigger game, medium ones worked rabbits alone or in packs, and small ones searched holes and rocks. Alert companionship links these varied working traditions.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Portuguese Podengo
sources.evidence: FCI utilization: large Podengo for big game, medium for rabbits alone or in packs, small for rabbit holes/rocks, all varieties watch and companion dogs. The FCI standard gives Portuguese hunting and watch use, three sizes, two coats, ears, tail, and adaptations to terrain.

VBO:0201067.historicalRoots: Portuguese warren and other hunting traditions.

VBO:0201087.summary: Calm and self-controlled between tasks, the Pudelpointer carries a strong hunting instinct into field, forest, and water. German breeders founded it from Poodle and Pointer stock to make a versatile pointing gun dog. Its breadth of terrain and steady manner together explain the purpose of that deliberate cross.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Pudelpointer
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Poodle–Pointer foundation and versatile field/forest/water work; temperament: calm, self-controlled, distinct hunting instinct, not game or gun shy. The FCI standard gives German origin, Poodle–Pointer foundation, separate breeding, rough coat and facial furnishings, and all-round field/wood/water work.

VBO:0201087.historicalRoots: German versatile gundog from Poodle and Pointer stock.

VBO:0201109.summary: Cooperative group hunting is a documented skill of Pungsan Dogs in Korea’s northern mountains. A university account describes several dogs surrounding large quarry and using barking to hold it in place until a hunter arrives. That coordinated behavior gives the breed a distinctive working tradition in difficult mountain country.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Pungsan Dog
sources.evidence: Kim Il Sung University agricultural-college account: northern Korean mountain hunting; describes dogs surrounding large game and barking until hunters arrive. The university agricultural-college article identifies a Korean mountain hunting dog with pale dense coat, erect ears, curled tail, cold adaptation, and national-dog designation.

VBO:0201125.summary: Curious and quick to learn, Rat Terriers can switch from friendly company to fearless, energetic hunting. American farmers prized their speed and persistence against rats and other small vermin. The breed’s sharp attention links that practical farm role with its lively household manner.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Rat Terrier
sources.evidence: UKC history/use: American farm vermin hunter; characteristics: energetic, alert, curious, intelligent, fearless and tenacious in hunting, friendly as companion. The UKC Rat Terrier standard describes U.S. farm and vermin roots, athletic smooth-coated form, ear carriage, and two size divisions.

VBO:0201141.summary: Calm and stable with familiar people, the Romanian Mioritic Shepherd Dog can show striking courage when a flock is threatened. It guarded livestock in the Carpathians against wolves, bears, and lynx while remaining wary of strangers near its charges. Long hours of mountain watch shaped its blend of composure and resolve.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Romanian Mioritic Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Carpathian flock dog and guard; temperament: calm, stable, courageous against wolf, bear and lynx, wary of strangers. The FCI standard gives Carpathian origins, herding and guarding roles, large long-coated form, and 1981 standard date; the Romanian breed name connects to sheep.

VBO:0201174.summary: Open, lively, and sociable with people, Samoyeds grew from a long partnership with northern Russian and Siberian communities. They helped with herding, hunting, and sledge travel, sometimes sharing shelter with the people beside whom they worked.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Samoyed
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: reindeer herding, hunting, sledding and shared shelters; temperament: friendly, open, alert, lively and social, little guarding instinct. The FCI standard describes northern Russian/Siberian roots, reindeer, hunting and sled roles, living close to people, medium white spitz form, and the smile expression.

VBO:0201174.historicalRoots: Northern Russian and Siberian sled and reindeer work.

VBO:0201184.summary: Alert and curious, Schipperkes tend to investigate closed doors, moving objects, and unfamiliar visitors, often sounding a sharp alarm. They grew from Flemish working communities as small guardians. Their name means “little shepherd,” a clue to roots deeper than the canal-barge story often attached to them.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Schipperke
sources.evidence: FCI history: Flemish working people, name means little shepherd; temperament: active, inquisitive, alert guard, barks in response to changes and reserved with strangers. The FCI standard gives Belgian/Flemish roots, seventeenth-century working-class history, name etymology, watchdog use, wedge head, ears, and black ruff.

VBO:0201198.summary: Loyal yet independent, the Scottish Terrier often meets the world with dignified reserve. Highland breeders valued the courage and intelligence needed to investigate quarry underground and keep working in difficult terrain.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Scottish Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI history: Scottish Highland terrier; temperament: loyal, faithful, dignified, independent, reserved, courageous and intelligent. The FCI standard gives Highland roots, 1882 club date, low powerful build, hard coat, long head, beard, and terrier work.

VBO:0201217.summary: Alert and responsive with familiar people, Shetland Sheepdogs can be more reserved on first meeting strangers. Their quick learning and attention to movement grew from island sheep work, even as the breed became a close companion. That persistent working focus remains one of their less visible qualities.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Shetland Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI use: companion and sheepdog; temperament: alert, gentle, intelligent, active, affectionate and responsive to owner, reserved with strangers. The FCI standard gives British/Shetland identity, sheepdog and companion use, small graceful outline, wedge head, mane, and double coat.

VBO:0201233.summary: Outgoing and gentle with people, Siberian Huskies often lack the suspicion expected of a guard dog. Their historic skill was teamwork in harness, moving light loads at a steady pace over great distances. Endurance and efficient cooperation, rather than guarding, define their working past.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Siberian Husky
sources.evidence: FCI use: long-distance light-load sled dog; temperament: friendly, gentle, alert, outgoing, not possessive or overly suspicious. The FCI standard gives Siberian sled work, light-load long-distance performance, compact medium frame, coat, ears, brush tail, and efficient gait.

VBO:0201242.summary: Strongly attached to their own people, Sloughis can also respond protectively when those people are threatened. Across North Africa they pursued game over open ground, drawing on keen chase instinct and sustained effort. Away from that work, this dignified sighthound is also noted for enjoying the comforts of home.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Sloughi
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: North African sighthound and sustained hunting; temperament: proud, attached to owner, protective if needed, appreciates home comfort. The FCI standard gives North African history, Moroccan patronage, sighthound use, lean elegant body, and short-coat-only status.

VBO:0201309.summary: Kindly in manner yet persistent on a scent, the Sussex Spaniel has a useful habit of giving voice while working thick cover. That call helps a hunter follow progress after the dog disappears into vegetation. The combination of steady determination and audible hunting sets it apart from quieter spaniels.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Sussex Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI use: flushing dog; temperament/work: gives tongue in thick cover, natural working ability, kindly disposition, rolling gait. The FCI standard gives flushing and voiced cover work, low strong form, golden-liver coat, and characteristic roll.

VBO:0201331.summary: Persistent across broken highland ground, the Taigan can join coordinated Kyrgyz hunts with a golden eagle. National kennel accounts describe pursuit of fox, ibex, and other game at elevations that challenge many coursing dogs. Mountain stamina and that unusual partnership give the breed a distinct working story.

sources.title: Official breed standard: Taigan
sources.evidence: VDH Taigan profile: Kyrgyz mountain sighthound working at 2,000–4,000 meters, quarry including fox and ibex, and coordinated hunting with golden eagles. The German kennel federation’s national Taigan profile gives Kyrgyz origin, sighthound classification, coat and feathering, hunting use, dimensions, and national recognition status.

VBO:0201351.summary: Protective of territory and closely loyal to familiar people, Tibetan Mastiffs tend to meet unfamiliar activity with serious watchfulness. Their Himalayan history includes guarding herds and monasteries, work that called for patience and independent judgment. The breed matures slowly; males may take four years or more to reach full development.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Tibetan Mastiff
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Himalayan nomad and monastery guardian; temperament: independent, protective, loyal to family/territory; males mature at least four years. The FCI standard gives Himalayan herder and monastery history, companion/watch/guard use, heavy coated form, mane, and slow maturity.

VBO:0201356.summary: Calm and affectionate with familiar people, Tornjaks can become formidable when guarding entrusted livestock or property. In the mountains of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, they watched flocks and farmyards while keeping a careful eye on strangers. Modern breeders rebuilt the type from scattered survivors of that older pastoral tradition.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Tornjak
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: mountain livestock and farm guard rebuilt from surviving stock; temperament: steady, affectionate with close people, vigilant, wary of strangers, quick to learn. The FCI standard gives Bosnian/Croatian mountain roots, livestock protection, near-square body, long coat, modern reconstruction, and medieval references.

VBO:0201356.interestingFact: Historical documents dated 1067 and 1374 mention dogs associated with the Tornjak’s region.
VBO:0201356.historicalRoots: Bosnian and Croatian mountain livestock protection.

VBO:0201389.summary: Friendly and eager to learn, the Vizsla tends to keep close contact with its handler through a hunt. It finds game, holds a point, and retrieves across Hungarian fields, forests, and water. That constant human partnership is one of its distinctive habits, grounded in a sporting history that reaches back through Magyar hunting traditions.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Vizsla
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Magyar and Hungarian sporting roots, versatile pointing/retrieving in field/forest/water; temperament: lively, friendly, trainable and keen to maintain contact with handler. The FCI standard gives Magyar/Carpathian history, fourteenth-century records, field/forest/water gundog work, and russet-gold short coat.

VBO:0201389.interestingFact: Hungarian documents and illustrations depicting the type reach back to the fourteenth century.
VBO:0201389.historicalRoots: Hungarian versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

VBO:0201411.summary: Active and merry, Welsh Springer Spaniels tend to be kindly with familiar people and persistent when searching cover. They flush game through rough vegetation in a Welsh sporting tradition separate from the English Springer’s. That patient, lively search is a distinctive skill behind their familiar companion manner.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Welsh Springer Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI use: Welsh flushing spaniel built for endurance and hard work; temperament: merry, very active and kindly; red-and-white coat. The FCI standard gives Welsh origin, flushing work, compact endurance build, red-and-white coat, head form, and energetic movement.

VBO:0201419.summary: Self-willed and watchful around the house, the Wetterhoun can be affectionate with familiar people yet reserved toward strangers. Around Friesland’s waterways it hunted otters and other small predators while also guarding the yard. Its local history even includes pulling small carts in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Wetterhoun
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Frisian otter hunting, yard watching and cart work; temperament: self-willed, affectionate with family, watchful, keen on vermin and initially reserved with strangers. The FCI standard gives Frisian origin, otter hunting and yard guarding, water-rich setting, cart work, square build, and curled coat.

VBO:0201419.historicalRoots: Frisian water hunting and farmyard work.

VBO:0201427.summary: Keenly attentive in the field and closely attached to familiar people, the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon also keeps watch over its territory. Eduard Korthals refined the breed as a versatile hunter that could point game and follow wounded larger quarry. Its broad field skills grew alongside that strong human partnership.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Wirehaired Pointing Griffon
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: Korthals development, pointing and wounded-large-game tracking; temperament: gentle, attached to owner and vigilant about territory. The FCI standard gives Korthals history, versatile pointing and tracking roles, rough coat, rectangular body, square muzzle, beard, and brows.

VBO:0201442.summary: Bold and energetic at work, Yakutian Laikas are also described as friendly and sociable with people. Communities of northeastern Russia relied on them as sled dogs and hunting partners through severe Arctic conditions. That joining of endurance and close human partnership has carried through a long regional history.

sources.title: FCI breed standard: Yakutian Laika
sources.evidence: FCI history/use: northeastern Russian sledding and hunting; temperament: bold, lively, energetic, friendly, sociable and close to people. The FCI standard gives northeast Russian aboriginal sled and hunting use, Arctic coat and build, and early regional written references.
